edges.description: Reactivated VZV spreads along sensory nerve fibers from the inflamed ganglion to infect keratinocytes in the innervated cutaneous dermatome.

edges.description: Lytic VZV infection of epidermal keratinocytes in the innervated dermatome produces the unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption.

edges.description: Sensitization of injured dermatomal sensory afferents produces cutaneous hyperesthesia and burning dysesthesia.

nodes.description: Two-dose recombinant subunit vaccine containing varicella-zoster virus glycoprotein E (gE) and the AS01B liposomal adjuvant system (MPL and QS-21). In phase 3 trials, HZ/su achieved 97.2% overall vaccine efficacy against herpes zoster in adults >=50 years of age (ZOE-50) and 91.3% efficacy against herpes zoster plus 88.8% efficacy against postherpetic neuralgia in adults >=70 years of age (pooled ZOE-50/ZOE-70), overcoming the age-related efficacy decline seen with live-attenuated zoster vaccine.
nodes.id: Adjuvanted Recombinant Zoster Vaccine (RZV / Shingrix, VZV gE + AS01B)

evidence.reference_title: Efficacy of an adjuvanted herpes zoster subunit vaccine in older adults.
evidence.snippet: During a mean follow-up of 3.2 years, herpes zoster was confirmed in 6 participants in the vaccine group and in 210 participants in the placebo group (incidence rate, 0.3 vs. 9.1 per 1000 person-years) in the modified vaccinated cohort. Overall vaccine efficacy against herpes zoster was 97.2% (95% confidence interval ... 93.7 to 99.0; P<0.001).

evidence.reference_title: Efficacy of the Herpes Zoster Subunit Vaccine in Adults 70 Years of Age or Older.
evidence.snippet: In pooled analyses of data from participants 70 years of age or older in ZOE-50 and ZOE-70 (16,596 participants), vaccine efficacy against herpes zoster was 91.3% (95% CI, 86.8 to 94.5; P<0.001), and vaccine efficacy against postherpetic neuralgia was 88.8% (95% CI, 68.7 to 97.1; P<0.001).

nodes.description: In a subset of patients, reactivated VZV spreads centripetally from sensory or cranial nerve ganglia into the spinal cord, leptomeninges, brain parenchyma, and cerebral arteries, causing VZV myelitis, meningitis, viral encephalitis, and cerebral vasculopathy.
nodes.id: Central Nervous System Extension of VZV

evidence.reference_title: The Spectrum of Neurological Manifestations of Varicella-Zoster Virus Reactivation.
evidence.snippet: Prominent among these conditions is a VZV vasculopathy, but the role of VZV in causing giant cell arteritis (GCA) is currently controversial. VZV reactivation can also cause segmental motor weakness, myelitis, cranial nerve syndromes, Guillain-Barre syndrome, meningoencephalitis, and zoster sine herpete, where a neurological syndrome occurs in the absence of the zoster rash.

evidence.reference_title: Can we forecast poor outcome in herpes simplex and varicella zoster encephalitis? A narrative review.
evidence.snippet: Less common manifestations of VZV reactivation, and rarely of primary infection, affect the CNS and peripheral nervous system (PNS). They include encephalitis, meningitis, cerebellitis, myelitis and vasculopathy/stroke as well as radiculopathy, peripheral facial palsy and Ramsay Hunt syndrome (18).

nodes.description: Following axonal delivery from the reactivated sensory ganglion to the innervated dermatome, VZV infects epidermal keratinocytes, modulating local antigen-presentation molecules (such as absent ICAM-1 and HLA-DR on VZV-infected keratinocytes alongside surrounding epidermal Th1 cytokine upregulation) and producing intraepidermal vesicular lesions.

evidence.reference_title: Absence of intercellular adhesion molecule 1 expression in varicella zoster virus-infected keratinocytes during herpes zoster: another immune evasion strategy?
evidence.snippet: HLA-DR and ICAM-1 expressions were not observed in VZV- and HSV-infected keratinocytes, contrasting with their upregulation in the surrounding epidermis and inside nonviral blisters.

evidence.reference_title: Varicella zoster virus infection.
evidence.snippet: Reactivation of the virus leads to virus replication, which causes zoster (shingles) in tissues innervated by the involved neurons, inflammation and cell death - a process that can lead to persistent radicular pain (postherpetic neuralgia).

nodes.description: Following primary varicella infection, VZV persists latently in dorsal root, trigeminal, geniculate, and autonomic ganglionic neurons. Immunosenescence or cellular immunosuppression allows latent VZV to reactivate, replicate within ganglionic neurons, and spread anterogradely down sensory axons to the corresponding cutaneous dermatome and central nervous system targets.
nodes.id: Ganglionic VZV Latency and Reactivation Under Waning T-Cell Immunity

evidence.reference_title: The Spectrum of Neurological Manifestations of Varicella-Zoster Virus Reactivation.
evidence.snippet: Varicella-Zoster virus (VZV) is a pathogenic human alpha herpes virus that causes varicella (chicken pox) as a primary infection and, following a variable period of latency in different ganglionic neurons, it reactivates to produce herpes zoster (shingles).

evidence.reference_title: Complications of varicella zoster virus reactivation.
evidence.snippet: With advancing age or immunosuppression, cell-mediated immunity to VZV declines and virus reactivates to cause zoster (shingles), which can occur anywhere on the body.

evidence.reference_title: Herpes Zoster Recurrence: A Narrative Review of the Literature.
evidence.snippet: The considerable healthcare burden of HZ is relatively well documented, with approximately one in three individuals experiencing at least one episode during their lifetime, debilitating symptoms including neuropathic pain, and complications such as post-herpetic neuralgia, vision loss, and rarely, stroke, and increased severity in immunocompromised individuals.

evidence.snippet: With the confirmed diagnosis of ZSH based on the skin sample, the patient was prescribed 3% lidocaine topical cream as needed, in addition to continuing with gabapentin. Over a few weeks, her radicular pain gradually improved, as observed during repeat cranial nerve examinations at subsequent close follow-up visits.

nodes.description: Systemic nucleoside analog antiviral therapy (oral acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir for uncomplicated acute herpes zoster; intravenous acyclovir for immunocompromised patients, ocular zoster, or central nervous system complications such as VZV vasculopathy, meningoencephalitis, and myelitis) accelerates rash healing and shortens acute zoster pain.

evidence.reference_title: Acyclovir for the prevention and treatment of varicella zoster in children, adolescents and pregnancy.
evidence.snippet: Early commencement of acyclovir is recommended for children with both varicella and altered cell mediated immunity, newborns during the first 2 weeks of life, preterm infants in the neonatal nursery, and severe varicella or shingles (including ocular zoster) in any patient, as well as during pregnancy.
